6.name: anticipates harder estate conflict

the harder part would not be conducted in her office or in the courthouse on Filbert Street but in this dining room

6.name: expects repeated dining room visits

evidence: she — Asha — would, against every rule she had set for herself about this case, be in that dining room more often than was strictly necessary

6.name: recalls matriarch's plea for kindness
6.description: Asha remembers the matriarch's February letter asking her children and housekeeper to be kind to one another in the room where she is gone.
evidence: because the matriarch had asked, in a letter written in February, for her children and her housekeeper to be kind to each other in the room where she was no longer standing

6.name: takes banker's box to call Halloran
6.description: Asha picks up the banker's box and goes to the front parlor to call Mr. Halloran.
evidence: She picked up the banker's box. She went into the front parlor to call Mr. Halloran.

6.name: hears family tension in dining room

evidence: Behind her, in the dining room, she heard Rosa say something very quietly in Spanish, and she heard Daniel answer, and she heard Lucia begin, at last, to cry.

6.description: Mr. Halloran answers Asha's call, and she tells him she has found a codicil.
evidence: Mr. Halloran picked up on the second ring.
"Asha. Tell me something kind."
"I have a codicil."

6.name: Halloran processes new information
6.description: Halloran pauses to absorb the news, showing the measured, intimidating style he is known for.
evidence: There was a pause on the line of the kind he was famous for
the sound of a man making space in his head for new information

6.name: identifies codicil witnesses

"By Rosa Maldonado, the housekeeper, and a Mrs. Inez Carra

evidence: "Witnessed."
"By Rosa Maldonado, the housekeeper, and a Mrs. Inez Carrasquillo, a neighbor on the block. Both signatures present. Dated February eleventh."

6.name: reveal will's equal thirds

evidence: "The house in equal thirds. Daniel, Lucia, Rosa. With a right of first refusal in favor of any beneficiary wishing to remain in residence, exercisable against the others at fair market value as established by independent appraisal."

6.name: report Daniel's reaction
6.description: Mr. Halloran asks how Daniel reacted, and Asha says Daniel asked her to stay for lunch.

"He asked me to stay for lunch."

6.name: decline Daniel's lunch invitation
6.description: Asha refuses Daniel's invitation to stay for lunch.

"Good girl."

"Marcus did. Three angles. And he's making a working copy now."

6.name: assess housekeeper's reliability

"She's the most reliable person in the house."

6.name: ask about the older one

"I know what you mean.\"

6.name: ask about the older child
6.description: Mr. Halloran asks Asha about the older child in the household.
evidence: "How's the older one.\"

6.name: assess Daniel's fear

6.name: ask about the younger child

6.description: Asha reflects that Lucia was right all along, had to be right alone, and now does not know how to handle being proven right aloud.
evidence: "She was right. She knew she was right. She had to be right alone in a house with people who told her she wasn't, for months, and now she gets to be right out loud, and she doesn't know what to do with that either."

6.name: insist she is fine
6.description: Asha insists that she is fine when Mr. Halloran asks about her.

"I'm fine, Mr. Halloran."
"I'm fine."

6.description: They settle into focused legal work, with Marcus typing and Asha dictating the petition in formal probate language.
evidence: They worked.
Marcus typed. She dictated.

The petition to lodge took shape on his screen in the careful, almost liturgical language of probate, language whose function was to flatten extraordinary domestic events into procedural inevitabilities.

6.name: Asha notices house is only partly heated

6.name: Asha and Marcus exchange a look
6.description: Asha and Marcus silently acknowledge Rosa's behavior by looking at each other.
evidence: "She's going to have to stop doing that," Marcus said quietly.

evidence: "You going to tell her."
"Not today."

6.name: Asha drinks the coffee

evidence: They drank the coffee. It was very good coffee, made in a way Asha did not know how to make coffee, with a faint sweetness in it that was not sugar.

6.name: Asha reflects on Rosa's long service
6.description: Asha thinks about Rosa's thirty-one years of learning the family's preferences and her current inheritance.
evidence: She thought about a woman who had stood in this kitchen for thirty-one years learning what each member of a family liked and not liked, and she thought about that woman now sitting in a dining room having been told she owned a third of the building

evidence: At a little past one she signed the petition.

6.description: As Asha leaves, she hears Lucia, Rosa, and Daniel talking quietly behind the closed dining room door.
evidence: The dining room door was closed now.
From behind it Asha could hear the low murmur of voices — Lucia's, mostly, and occasionally Rosa's, and once Daniel's, not arguing, just speaking.

6.name: Asha leaves without listening

evidence: She did not stop to listen.
She let Marcus open the front doo

6.name: Asha leaves the house with Marcus

evidence: Asha could hear the low murmur of voices — Lucia's, mostly, and occasionally Rosa's, and once Daniel's, not arguing, just speaking. She did not stop to listen. She let Marcus open the front door and she stepped out onto the stoop

6.name: Cold air shocks Asha outside
6.description: The February air hits Asha as she stands blinking on the top step.
evidence: the February air took her like a slap and she stood there for a second on the top step blinking at the brightness of it

6.name: Marcus offers to drive
6.description: Marcus asks if he should drive, and Asha agrees.
evidence: "You want me to drive," Marcus said.
"Please."

6.name: Marcus drives Asha to the office
6.description: Marcus drives east on Spruce toward the office without turning on the radio.
evidence: In the car, heading east on Spruce toward the office, Marcus did not turn on the radio, which was his small mercy.

6.name: Asha reflects on the letter and Daniel's invitation
6.description: Asha thinks about the letter in the banker’s box, Rosa's gesture, Daniel's lunch invitation, and her need to be careful about mistaking relief for permission.
evidence: Asha put her head back against the seat and closed her eyes and let the city slide past her in the dark behind her eyelids.
She thought about the letter in the banker's box on the back seat.
She thought about Rosa's hand pressing flat against the table.

She thought about Daniel asking her to stay for lunch and about the particular tone in which he had asked, which had been the tone of a man asking for something he had not known he was allowed to want, and she thought about how careful she was going to have to be, in the weeks ahead, not to mistake the relief of being asked for the permission to say yes.

6.name: Asha asks Marcus to warn her
6.description: Asha asks Marcus to tell her if she starts spending too much time at that house.
evidence: "Marcus."
"If I start spending too much time at that house, tell me."

6.description: Marcus promises to tell Asha and to keep warning her even if she ignores him at first.
evidence: "I will."
"Promise me."
"I promise you," Marcus said, "that I will tell you, and I also promise you that you will not listen the first time, and I promise you that I will tell you again."

6.description: Asha gives a brief, nearly silent laugh in response to Marcus's promise.
evidence: She laughed once, short, almost soundless.

evidence: ill tell you, and I also promise you that you will not listen the first time, and I promise you that I will tell you again."

6.name: she laughs at his remark
6.description: She responds with a brief, nearly silent laugh, signaling dry amusement or resignation.
evidence: She laughed once, short, almost soundless.

evidence: "I know it's about right. I've worked for you for six years."

6.name: they drive in silence

evidence: They made the rest of the drive in silence.

evidence: At the office she went straight to Mr. Halloran's door and laid the petition on his desk and the original codicil, in its archival sleeve, on top of the petition.

6.description: Mr. Halloran studies the codicil carefully, reading it twice before speaking.

6.description: Halloran identifies the codicil as clean and self-proving, confirming its legal strength.

"Self-proving."
"Yes."

"I think he had the access, the motive, and the temperament. I cannot yet say he had the act."

6.description: Halloran asks whether she will investigate the missing codicil, and she hesitates before answering.

She thought about this. She had thought about it, in fact, all the way down Spruce Street, and she had not yet arrived at an answer that satisfied her.

6.name: she declines immediate investigation
6.description: She decides not to pursue the missing-codicil question yet because the codicil has already been filed and the will amended of record.
evidence: "Not yet," she said.

"The codicil is filed. The will is amended of record. The disposition of the house is now governed by an instrument that reflects, by every indication available to me, the actual final intent of the decedent. To prosecute the question of how the codicil came to be missing woul

To prosecute the question of how the codicil came to be missing would be to introduce a criminal allegation into a probate that has just, against considerable odds, stabilized itself.
I would prefer to leave the question available rather than to ask it.

6.name: Halloran questions who may accuse

"To the sister. To the housekeeper. To Daniel himself, eventually, if he wants to give an account of it. It is their inheritance. It is their accusation to make or to set down."

6.description: Halloran reflects that Asha's position is either wise or tender, signaling his uncertainty about her motives.

evidence: "Go home, Asha."
"It's two in the afternoon."

"Go home anyway. Or go for a walk. Or sit in a café with a book. Tomorrow you are going to spend the morning in that dining room mediating a fair-market appraisal among three people who an hour ago discovered they own a house together, and you are going to need to be a person and not a function when you do it. Go."
